lede: Puritan Cape Cod, Hyannis and Mashpee.
items: Two more Puritan Cape Cod doors join the index — the Hyannis flagship at 408 Main Street, trading since 1939 in the old post office, and Mashpee Commons — beside the Chatham store already on file. The chain merchandises as one, so all three carry the same fifteen of the map’s brands. The index goes to 153 shops.

lede: The Stores index opens as a directory.
items: Regions open collapsed — 46 headers with their counts under nine states, the whole Northeast on one screen — and expand in place with a tap. The filter box expands whatever it matches. “open ›” beside a region takes it to its own page, with the route.

lede: Three Bostons become three streets.
items: When a brand has more than one door in a town, the segments carry the street: Lululemon reads Boston · Newbury Street, Boston · Congress Street, Boston · Boylston Street. A hundred brand-and-town pairs on the map have more than one door.

lede: Quieter pills, clearer counts.
items: The arrows come off the store pills; the strip’s label says once that a tap opens the store in Maps. A region view now reads “4 stores in Lehigh Valley” with a link to all 808 in the Northeast, rather than “4 of 808 stores”, which read as if the region held them all.

lede: An expanded pill is one capsule.
items: When a brand with several doors is expanded, the brand and its towns sit in one outlined capsule: the brand at the left (tap to close), a Maps segment per town, and the brand page as the last segment. The towns no longer float beside a second copy of the name.

lede: A brand-owned store pill opens the door in Maps.
items: A pill for a single store opens that store in Google Maps. A brand with several doors in a region — Vineyard Vines ×2 — expands in place to one Maps pill per town, with the brand’s name linking to its page. Where is the door, in one tap.

lede: Brand-owned stores, named as such.
items: “Brand stores” are now “brand-owned stores” everywhere — the filter, the counts, the rows, and the chip strip, which reads “Brand-owned stores in South Shore” rather than “here”. The distinction the page draws is between a store the brand runs itself and an independent shop that buys from many brands, and the words now say so.

lede: State, region, store — in that order.
items: The Stores page reads top-down now. A state is a serif heading with a rule; a region is a smaller serif heading; a store is a sans row, set in from the region. Region headings had been smaller than the store names beneath them, which put the list upside down.

lede: Close takes you back to where you were.
items: Closing a brand page returns you to what you opened it from — the Stores index, with its filter and region intact, or a shop page, or a brand’s region panel — instead of the home page.
The brand-store chips in each region now sit under their own label, “Brand stores here”, with a rule above them, so they no longer read as part of the last shop’s row.

lede: Brand-store chips in the store’s own case.
items: A small fix: the brand-store chips had inherited capital letters from the link style they open with.

lede: The Stores page is organised by region.
items: Stores open by region, under their state — South Shore, Cape, Fairfield County — each with a count and its route, so a reader sees what is near them before what begins with A. The A-to-Z list is one tap away.

Brand stores collapse to a chip per brand. A Faherty in Hingham is the same as a Faherty in Nantucket; within a region the brand’s doors are now one chip with a count, the towns in the tooltip, opening the brand’s page. Independent shops keep full rows, because each is different.
A filter box narrows the page as you type — a name, a town, a state, a region.
Each independent shop leads with what it carries: three of the map’s brands and a count, so Louie can be told from Miltons without opening either.

lede: Club Monaco leaves the map.
items: Club Monaco is unseated. Its men’s range has all but gone from its own store — one trouser, sold out and final sale; one sweater — and a house with no men’s rail to send a reader to cannot hold a seat. It goes to the bench with the reason, and comes back if the range does. The map holds 203 brands.

lede: Garment labels open the brand’s own men’s pages across the map.
items: 1,270 garment links on 193 brands, each read on the brand’s own US store between 19 and 21 September with the tiles checked for men’s product. 143 brands carry the own pages mark: every priced garment opens the right men’s listing. Elsewhere a label still opens site search, and its tooltip says so.

Thirty-three site-search links that went nowhere are gone. A sixth of the map’s shopping links had rotted — stores that moved, locales that changed — and a label with no working link is now plain text rather than a dead one.

Seven store domains corrected to the brand’s real US storefront: J.Lindeberg, Isaia, Kiton, Isabel Marant, Baracuta, Peserico, Sid Mashburn. Five luxury houses still block every reader; Comme des Garçons, Junya Watanabe, Charvet and Sugar Cane have no store to link.

lede: You can see which brands’ garment labels open their own pages.
items: An own pages mark sits beside Prices on a card or brand page when every priced garment links to the brand’s own men’s listing. Seven brands carry it so far: Lululemon, Faherty, Outerknown, Todd Snyder, J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, Brunello Cucinelli. Elsewhere a label still opens the brand’s site search, and its tooltip says so. A solid underline is an own page; a dotted one is a search.

lede: Room for the range tag.
items: The price table’s value column is wider so a figure and its range tag fit on one line.

lede: Every price state is drawn, and garment labels open the brand’s own men’s listing.
items: A price read in another currency is shown as read and never converted. Ring Jacket’s outerwear reads ¥385,000–440,000 and draws no bar, because a yen figure cannot sit on a dollar axis. Eleven brands were showing “not assessed” for prices that had been read.
“None published” is a state. A brand that publishes no price anywhere says so, distinct from a garment nobody looked at and from a garment it does not make.

Range bars are marked. Seventy-four brands sell no loafer, or no jacket in two cloths, so their bar is the cheapest-to-dearest of the category rather than the entry-to-elevated pair. Those bars now carry a small range tag and read lighter.
Garment labels open the brand’s own men’s listing — Polo goes to the polos, not a site search that mixes genders. Seven brands so far; the rest as the links are read.

Forty-two shoe cells and six sweater cells go back to “not assessed”. They had been filed as “does not make it” because the brand sells no loafer or no crewneck; a house that sells shoes does make shoes. They restate as ranges.

lede: Ninety-nine price rows restated on the rulings of the 18th.
items: The outerwear pair is now the same jacket in an entry and an elevated cloth wherever a brand sells one — Levi’s trucker at $90 in denim and $1,200 in shearling, Filson’s at $199 and $1,199 — and the four highs that had counted mink, vicuña, alligator or sharkskin are restated without them, along with seven more the thread found on its own. Sub-lines sold under the brand’s name now count: Fear of God’s ESSENTIALS, Margiela’s MM6, Rick Owens’s DRKSHDW. Celine and Fedeli are read. 193 brands now have all eight garments settled; Saint Laurent, Gucci, Balenciaga and Bottega Veneta still block every reader we have.

lede: Sweaters, outerwear and shoes are priced for most of the map.
items: 128 more brands carry sweater, outerwear and shoe prices, read off their own US stores at full price on 18 September with the product behind every figure on file; 176 brands now have all eight garments settled. Twenty-eight brands gained a working link to their own site search, so their garment labels shop. Sixteen brands are held: eight price in yen, euros, pounds or duty-paid dollars that cannot share an axis with a US list price; four had a fur or exotic-skin piece counted as the high and will be restated; four have no store to read.

The vendor field lied at nine more houses. Southern Tide, Faherty, Percival, Kith, Norse Projects, NN07, Alex Mill, Sease and J.Press list other makers’ footwear under their own name; at J.Press it is inverted, with own-label knits carrying the maker as vendor.

lede: Seven more brands priced to all eight garments.
items: Todd Snyder, J.Crew, Polo Ralph Lauren, Brunello Cucinelli, Margaret Howell, Barbour and Saint James now carry sweater, outerwear and shoe prices read off their own stores at full price, with the product behind every figure on file. Margaret Howell’s shoes are Dr. Martens and Mizuno under its own label, so its shoe row says does not make rather than showing a price. Auralee’s figures are held: its US-region prices include duties and are not list prices.

lede: Routes appear only in a region view.
items: The full index no longer offers a route. With 808 stores it had become 81 legs of ten, a wall of pills nobody would drive. Tap a region and its route is there as before.

lede: Brand-store rows read like the others.
items: A typographic fix: brand-store rows in the index had picked up the styling of the brand-page link they open, and read heavier than the shop rows beside them.

lede: Boutiques becomes Stores, and the brands’ own doors join the index.
items: The index now lists every store in the Northeast the map knows about — 151 independent shops and 657 brand-owned stores — A to Z, each tagged by region, with a filter for all, independent shops only, or brand stores only. A brand store opens the brand’s page; an independent shop opens its own. Region views and their Google Maps routes follow the filter.

Fifty-five more towns are mapped to regions so the brand stores could carry tags, and Western New York and Central New York join the list. Nine brand-store town names were tidied — three spellings of East Hampton, four of New York — so they map at all.

lede: Tap a garment in the price strip to shop it.
items: Every priced garment label on a card or brand page is a link to the brand’s own site search for that garment — tap Polo and you are on the brand’s polos. It works for the 167 brands whose site search is on file; the label stays plain where it is not. The Shoes row carries the curated shoe link where one exists, so the separate Shoes line on the card is gone. The fabric link under the description stays; it points at what the brand is built on rather than at a garment.

lede: The cards that appear while you drag a dial can be read to the end on a phone.
items: On a phone, the card panel no longer scrolls inside itself. The inner scroll box was a fix for a desktop drag problem, and on a phone it trapped the cards: the page would not move past the panel and the bottom of a card could not be reached. The page now grows instead.

lede: The card's lead line says three things, not ten.
items: The line under a brand’s name on the card is now three clauses at most: what the house leads with, what it is built on, and the one register that most sets it apart. “National reach”, “works in both” and “accommodating” were true of nearly everyone and said nothing; they stay on the full page. Loro Piana went from eleven clauses to three: comfort and craft first · built on cashmere and wool · dressed for a boat you do not drive.

lede: Fifteen range lines settled.
items: Sid Mashburn, Brooks Brothers, Zegna and Proper Cloth restate with socks out and underwear in, now that a combined socks-and-underwear category is split by the garment. Ksubi restates on its US range rather than the Australian one. Eleven other houses carry completed category lists. Scotch & Soda is held: the house publishes two compositions that disagree on 24 styles, and its row waits for one reading that settles everything together.

lede: The Cape is one region and each island is its own.
items: Cape and Islands becomes three: The Cape (Chatham, Orleans, Provincetown), Martha’s Vineyard (Edgartown, Vineyard Haven) and Nantucket. A route to the Vineyard and a route to Nantucket are different days, and the tags now say so.

lede: Woodbury is on Long Island.
items: Woodbury Mens Shop moves from Hudson Valley to Long Island. Its address is Jericho Turnpike, Nassau County; the tag had been assigned from the town name and there are two Woodburys in New York.

lede: A region becomes a route.
items: Every region view carries a button that opens its shops as a Google Maps route. Stops are ordered by postcode as a starting point and can be dragged in Maps. Google takes ten stops per route, so the Cape and Islands’ twelve shops arrive as two legs.

lede: Region tags open the region.
items: Tap a region tag — on the index or on a shop’s page — and the index shows that region’s shops together, with a link back to all of them. The address bar follows, so a region is a link you can send.

lede: The boutiques index reads A to Z, and every shop carries its region.
items: The index is alphabetical. It had been grouped by state and then by town, which suited a map and not a list; a shop is now found by its name, and the previous and next buttons on every shop page follow the same order.

Every shop is tagged with its region — South Shore, Cape and Islands, MetroWest, Fairfield County, Hudson Valley, Main Line and Chester County and thirty-odd more — on the index and on its own page. The tags come from one table of towns; a town that is not in it cannot be published.

lede: Louie joins the index.
items: Louie, South Weymouth, is a stockist for sixteen of the map’s brands — Barbour, Herno, Ring Jacket, RRL, Polo Ralph Lauren, RLX, Merz b. Schwanen, John Smedley, Saint James, Sunspel, Wax London, Valstar, Gran Sasso, Rodd & Gunn, Criquet and Borgo28 — read from the house’s own brand list. It is the clothing shop the LaRossa family added beside LaRossa Shoe, founded 1923, on Columbian Square. The index goes to 151 shops.

lede: The range is clothing only.
items: Hats, socks, belts, bags and shoes leave the count — 5,238 styles across 68 brands. The range now describes what a man wears, not everything a house sells. Carhartt is the biggest move: 1,472 styles with 793 licensed caps that state nothing, to 361 styles at 90% disclosed and 62% natural. Socks were the stretch at six houses; Wythe’s performance-stretch share goes to zero.

Two stretch figures were wrong before scope touched them and are corrected. Lacoste’s had been read off collar ribs and plackets, not the cloth; Charles Tyrwhitt’s counted 48 cotton shirts with “mechanical stretch” and no elastane.

Lululemon’s stretch is not yet counted at this scope. Its site refused every request for two and a half hours; the range splits are in, the stretch cells wait for a retry rather than publish a number known to be too high.

lede: The range is measured for 198 brands, and the natural-fibre dial stops being a prototype.
items: 73,908 men’s styles were counted on 191 brands’ own product pages, joining the seven measured earlier. Every card now says how the range divides — natural, synthetic and, where it matters, cellulosic — and how much of it stretches. Four houses publish no composition anywhere (Sugar Cane, Junya Watanabe, Charvet, Cesare Attolini); two are held short of a full read (Hermès, Eleventy).

Cellulosics are a third figure. Rayon, viscose, modal and lyocell are neither cotton nor polyester, and folding them into either side misdescribes a house. PAIGE is 34% cellulosic; on the old two-way count it would have read as a 99% natural denim house.

Stretch is two numbers. How much of the range has any elastane, and how much has 5% or more. Brioni has 43 elastane styles and none at 5%; State & Liberty runs 78% of its range at 5% or more. Comfort stretch and performance stretch were one figure and are now two.
The natural-fibre dial is derived from the count for 195 brands, banded on the styles that state a composition, and not assessed where fewer than half do. It is no longer marked as a prototype.
Rothy’s counts zero — it sells no men’s clothing — and the card says so rather than saying nothing.

lede: Golfiness is back on the rail.
items: The Golfiness dial returns, at the top of Culture. It measures how much golf runs the brand — Rhoback, Criquet, TravisMathew, Malbon, Redvanly and Peter Millar at 5, thirty brands scored in all. Golffice stays as the two-way dial for course against office; the two answer different questions and both were needed.

lede: The card opens at the top, links to the full page from the top, and the brand page leads with the words.
items: The brand page now opens with the summary, origin and the house's own words, then the stores, then the prices. The dials and registers follow. Reading before measuring.
On a phone, every card now opens at the top. The sheet had been keeping the scroll position of the last card, so the next brand opened part-way down with its name hidden.
The link to the full brand page sits at the top of the card, beside the close button, instead of at the foot.

lede: Brand and stockist pages page along the spectrum, and the site is built from data rather than edited by hand.
items: Previous and next on every brand page and every stockist page. A brand page steps along the spectrum in the order the chips are drawn, skipping anything the active filters have put out, and says where it is (“48 of 204”, or “12 of 31 shown” under a filter). A stockist page steps through the boutiques index — by state, then city, then name. The arrow keys do the same.

The page is now a build. The 204 brand records, the 807 places, the rubric and the changelog live in a data folder, one file per brand, checked by a registry that says what every field is and what its absence means. The page you are reading is assembled from them. Nothing about what it shows changed; a lot about how it can change did.

lede: The register reaches New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Delaware, and the region it describes is now the Northeast.
items: Thirty-two Mid-Atlantic shops join the index, which goes from 116 to 148 across nine states. Boyds in Philadelphia carries twenty-four of the map’s brands, Larrimor’s in Pittsburgh and Weitzenkorn’s in Pottstown fifteen each. Eighty-nine brands gain a stockist they did not have.
The region is renamed. It began as New England and New York and now runs ten states from Maine to Delaware, so every panel, caveat and heading says the Northeast instead.

New Jersey and Pennsylvania rendered as bare two-letter codes in the index, because both state-name maps stopped at New York. The suite now asserts that every state the register can hold has a full name, and that no shop renders a code.

Ninety-seven of the 129 doors found in the region are recorded and not yet in the index: their brand lists need a phone call rather than a fetch. Two that looked complete were not — a paginated brands page returned its first page to every static fetch, showing twenty-four of one shop’s hundred and twenty-five brands.

C’H’C’M’ on Bond Street joins the register, and carries two of the map’s brands out of twenty-eight. That is the lowest ratio of any shop on file — Boyds carries twenty-four, Richards twenty-one — and it is not a judgement on the shop. It is a shop buying almost entirely outside what the map covers: Evan Kinori, Arpenteur, MAN-TLE, Teatora, Hender Scheme. The twenty-six it stocks and the map does not are now a seating candidate list, chosen by a buyer rather than by a search.

Four seated: Robert Talbott, Duck Head, Saint James and Borgo28. Talbott began in a converted Carmel garage in 1950 making bow ties for the Del Monte Golf Club and still leads with the necktie. Duck Head is 1865 Nashville, named for the duck canvas it was cut from, dormant for years and revived by Oxford Industries. Saint James has been spinning wool in the Normandy town of the same name since 1889 and has been employee-owned since 1990.

Five of eight product ranges hide their real size behind colourways, in five different encodings. Duck Head puts the colour after a dash, so 196 of 197 titles are unique and a title-level dedup returns 197 against a true 90. And a worse trap surfaced: any extractor returning the same country on every style is reading page furniture rather than product data — Robert Talbott showed made in America on 85 of 85 from a navigation link, against a true 8 of 85 with Türkiye largest.

kloTH, Hingham — a womenswear boutique with a five-brand menswear tail, captured in person rather than from a locator. Three of the five are on the map. It is the second independent in Hingham and the register’s first entry sourced entirely from a visit.

lede: A natural-fibre dial that is counted rather than judged, and a line on the card saying how a brand’s range divides.
items: Natural fibre joins the rail, measured. Every score is a count of styles by main fibre read from the brand’s own product pages — 85% or more of the range is a 5. Six houses are counted so far and the rest read as not assessed, which on this map has never meant zero.

Push natural and tech up together and Peter Millar is the only house that answers. That is the point of the pair: 46% natural against 45% synthetic, and the two halves are separate lines rather than blends.

The card now says how a range divides. Peter Millar’s polos, pullovers and shorts run synthetic while its sweaters and sport coats are natural — kept apart rather than blended. Loro Piana reads natural throughout with no synthetic line beside it, on 675 styles and zero synthetics. A house at synthetics 4 and wool 3 could be either of those, and they are opposite things to expect on walking in.
The dial counts cotton and cashmere alike, which is why J.Crew at 90% outranks Loro Piana at 86%. Which fibre a house favours is what the four dials above it are for.

Swim, boxers and lounge count toward the fibre totals and not toward the verdict on how a range divides. Every house’s swimwear is synthetic by physical necessity, and counting it made two natural houses read as split ones.

Eighty-seven store addresses were captured a week ago and never merged. Sixteen brands with stores in the Northeast were saying nothing about them — Brooks Brothers in eighteen towns, Banana Republic in nineteen, Todd Snyder in ten — while the addresses sat in the capture files unread. They are in now, and the regional panels list them. Nine brands still have counts without addresses and the card says so rather than staying silent, because a brand with stores and no addresses on file used to read exactly like a brand with no stores at all. Forty-five remain silent, which for them is the truth.

Brunello Cucinelli is complete at last. It was the only brand on the map with a count and no addresses, held since the first locations pass because its source file left the city column blank on sixty-three of sixty-four rows. The city was in the store name all along — SCOTTSDALE, BEVERLY HILLS, CARMEL — and the thirty-four own boutiques now sit in thirty-three towns, with thirty Saks and Neiman Marcus concessions excluded. Every brand on the map now has a door record and none is count-only.

Levi’s had 458 US stores on record and has 97. A capture of the brand’s own directory found 259 locations, of which 160 are outlets — recorded and not counted, on the rule that took Brooks Brothers from 138 to 54. Where the 458 came from is not recoverable; it predates the current location work and nothing supports it. Thirteen own stores fall in the Northeast, including Boston Seaport, Derby Street and MarketStreet Lynnfield. Pittsburgh was on file and has no Levi’s store of any format.

Seven brands were reporting no stores in the region while the map held their addresses. Canali read 0 own stores, 11 stockists with two of its shops — one on Madison Avenue — sitting in the capture files unmerged. The regional record existed for the stockists alone, so the check added this morning never fired: it asked whether a brand had a record, when it should have asked whether that record had any stores in it. Thirteen more addresses are in, and a brand whose own-door list is empty now falls back to the door count like any other.

Merz b. Schwanen seated, 201st — and the register grew by sixteen shops on the same visit. The Albstadt house has run since 1911 and was shut down by the founder’s descendants; Gitta and Peter Plotnicki found a ninety-year-old Henley at a Berlin flea market in 2011, were offered the name, and spent a year restoring the machines. Thirty-two loopwheelers are still running, the oldest built in 1889. Its 119 clothing styles are 97% natural fibre and carry no elastane at all — the only stretch anywhere in the range is a swim lining and one sock. It sells no jeans, no dress shirts and no shoes, all checked rather than assumed.

Seating a brand is now also a way to find shops. Merz’s locator held 420 stockists across 38 countries, and diffing the 89 US entries against the register turned up twenty-one in the Northeast that the map did not have. Sixteen qualify as independent clothing shops and are in; the others are a cobbler, a garden shop, an outdoor-gear chain and two womenswear boutiques. The boutiques index goes from 100 to 116.

The totals were wrong in five different ways. BOSS’s 74 and Sandro’s 45 counted department-store concessions — 147 and 37 of them. Diesel’s 24 counted ten outlets. Club Monaco’s 39 and Scotch & Soda’s 7 described fleets that no longer exist. J.Crew’s 114 was the right number of stores and seven of its towns had closed while seven towns with a store were missing. Mizzen+Main had four on record and has ten.

Southern Tide’s stores were written with full state names rather than codes on all thirty-nine towns, so they matched no state filter anywhere on the map — five of them in Chatham, Mashpee, Nantucket, Newport and Westport, which should have been in the regional panel and were invisible to it. Normalised, and the suite now asserts that every door record and every addressed place uses a two-letter code.
top: Every brand on the map now has a complete US store record. 201 of 201, no partials and no counts without addresses, on 3,481 addressed stores. The last eleven came back with 1,062 rows and not one of the totals they were checked against survived intact.

Three brands have no US store at all. Club Monaco’s American fleet closed through 2025 and its own locator now lists eleven Canadian stores and a Bally co-branded shop; Scotch & Soda’s US directory no longer serves pages and its last store is closed; Zilli lists twenty-two countries and the United States is not among them. All three were carrying 39, 7 and an unknown.

Fourteen of Dior’s thirty-six US boutiques sell no menswear — including Manhasset and Greene Street — so the map counts twenty-two. A menswear map had been counting womenswear shops as stores since the first locations pass, and nothing in the record could have shown it: the finding came from reading each store page’s own categories.

lede: Twenty-six more brands checked, and the record turns out to be worse than the first pass suggested.
top: Of 103 figures that could be compared, one was right. Robert Barakett's dress pants, correct to the dollar. Ten more priced a garment the house does not make, and seven said a garment did not exist when it does — Eton sells both tees and polos, Vuori sells jeans, Mott & Bow makes no shirts at all.
43 brands now carry a checked mark, up from 18.

The new slots are carrying houses the five-slot map could not describe. Johnstons of Elgin has 111 jumpers between $725 and $1,795 and was previously represented by a t-shirt cell. Barbour's 208 jackets give the Bedale, its one thing, somewhere to live at last.

items: A five-pocket silhouette is not evidence of denim. Eight non-denim five-pockets turned up — linen at 120% Lino, Versaknit at Cuts, stretch twill at Robert Barakett, and at Marine Layer two of them priced above the real jeans.
Barbour's recorded jeans band bracketed a denim shirt, which is the same failure that put Hartford's shirts in its jeans cell.

The shoes dial has three false zeros, not one. Robert Barakett runs a footwear heading with 40 Italian-made shoes priced above everything it sells but one jacket, and Ring Jacket has a shoes category. Three wrong of six checked.
Four brands run permanent sitewide sales with the discount in the prominent position, and Sandro sorts by the discounted price — so reading the extremes gives $52.50 against a list floor of $155.
Eleven figures are the brand's own list price in euros or yen — Fedeli and Ring Jacket. Real findings, held until they can share an axis with a dollar.
Five cells are held on their own merits, including Fedeli's polo band, which reads winter knits because the piqué polo it is known for is out of season and off the site entirely.

Following a brand from a shop page opened out of the boutiques index left the index sitting over the brand card. The rule that clears anything stacked above the card was a hand-kept list of three overlays and the index had never been added to it — the comment above it said every new overlay must be listed there, which is a comment doing a job the code should do. The stack is now read from the document in z-index order, so a view added later cannot be forgotten.

Every hover card was printing three rows reading undefined beneath its price strip. When the map went from five garments to eight, four label arrays needed extending and only three were found; the fourth drove the hover card alone, so the fault was invisible on the brand card and the prices overlay and present on all two hundred hovers. The suite now asserts on every label array at once rather than on whichever one turns up in a search.

The scandi man rubric claimed a passport was neither required nor sufficient. The scores say otherwise — every brand at 3 or above is Nordic and the ceiling for a non-Nordic house is 2 — so the dial is a geographic register like italianness and frenchness, and now says so. A reader seeing a Swedish house at 2 should be able to tell that is a judgement about its register rather than an error.

Peserico, 199th. A Veneto house founded in 1962 on women’s trousers, whose menswear arrived only in 2021 — recorded plainly, because a five-year-old line inside a sixty-four-year-old womenswear company is something a reader should not have to discover. It earns wool 5 on an unusual basis: it names its mills, which almost no house does, and the list is Loro Piana, Vitale Barberis Canonico, Reda and Zegna Baruffa Lane Borgosesia.

Malbon, 200th. Founded in Los Angeles in 2017 by Stephen and Erica Malbon as an Instagram account, then a Fairfax Avenue storefront that doubled as a clubhouse for golfers, skaters and artists. It joins TravisMathew as only the second brand on the map at the course pole of golffice — there is no office half to it at all — and it reaches golf from streetwear rather than from apparel, its founder having come out of the cult magazine Frank151.

Peserico’s eight cells are filled, and the check found the men’s range was more than twice the size it appeared: a second, undiscounted autumn collection of 98 pieces sitting alongside the 66 on sale, with no overlap between them. The ceiling moved from $1,629 to $2,005 and the shoe cell exists at all only because of it.

Malbon’s eight cells are filled, and two of them are the interesting ones. It sells no jeans at all — the only denim-named trousers are chambray in a golf-pant cut — so the cell is a checked absence rather than a guess. And its shoe range is three of its own silhouettes among twenty-eight listings: the rest are adidas, New Balance, FootJoy, Red Wing, XtraTuf and a Jimmy Choo slide, all carrying Malbon in the vendor field. Read at face value that gives a $125–750 Malbon shoe business which is really five other houses.

Both new houses have their US stores on record, every address checked against an independent map listing rather than against the brand’s own locator. Peserico keeps eight of its nineteen: the other eleven are concessions inside Bloomingdale’s and Saks, and the map does not count a concession as an own store — the rule that closed Paul & Shark. Malbon has ten, two more than the eight its press reported. Four Peserico boutiques and one Malbon store fall inside the Northeast and now appear in the regional panels.

The dial now measures how technical the clothes are, not who invented them. A membrane keeps the rain out whoever owns the patent, so a house selling licensed Gore-Tex is selling technical clothing. Ownership decides only the last step: a 5 is a house that developed what it sells, a 4 is a house selling something as technical under licence. Sease sits at 4 on serious outerwear that is all Loro Piana’s; Mizzen+Main joins it, four licensed technologies against two of its own; Vollebak keeps its 5 having named nothing, because it went and found the graphene.

Four of the nine brands at the top of the dial were wrong, and the dial was measuring the wrong thing. Every tech score was assigned from brand summaries before this project could look at what a house sells. Thirty-six were audited blind against named technologies, technical filters and their counts, with each technology marked as the house’s own or licensed from someone else.

Naming a fabric is not owning a technology. Redvanly has thirty house-named cloths — PUREpoly is polyester, ComfortChino is chino, Activedenim is denim — and drops from 5 to 3. Vollebak names no technology at all and holds its 5, because the material is the name: graphene, aramid, ceramic, aerogel and copper. Counting house names would have inverted both.

Patagonia rises to 5, the deepest house technology of the thirty-six: its own product families, its own warmth index and eighteen technical filters. Rakho falls to 1, nothing named across eighty-four products.

Peserico rises to 2 — named weather finishes on a line of technical wool outerwear, under a cloth-and-tailoring argument. Malbon settles at 3: licensed Coolcore and Gore-Tex across a modest part of the range.

The rubric gained a third case. It had a house that develops what it sells at 5 and a house selling licensed technology at 4, and no home for a house selling ordinary performance cloth under its own fabric names. A full read of Peter Millar’s 581 product pages settled it: 197 of 352 men’s styles are synthetic, 199 carry spandex, and the house’s own filter counts match the fibre content rather than overstating it — but Summer Comfort, across 51 products, is 92% polyester with spandex, and no licensed technology appears anywhere. Depth of technical product now drives the scale and ownership decides only whether a house can reach the top.

groups.t: Two houses read fibre by fibre
items: Peter Millar and Todd Snyder are near-opposites, and reading every product page of both is what showed it. Peter Millar’s clothing is 56% synthetic with spandex in 57% of styles, built on its own fabric names over stock stretch blends. Todd Snyder’s is 3% synthetic, with spandex in 12% at one to three per cent for comfort, and 377 of its 600 styles are a single fibre.

They make opposite claims about cloth. Peter Millar names fabrics it owns and no mills; Todd Snyder names no fabrics and states where the cloth comes from on 321 styles — Italy on 195, and 33 of its 39 sport coats. Every mill it names belongs to somebody else.

Peter Millar is two lines, not a blend. Its polyester and its wool sit in different categories rather than in the same garment: the polos are 92% polyester, the sweaters and sport coats are wool and cashmere. That is a different thing to walk in expecting from a house that blends, and the two read identically on the dials as they stand.

Todd Snyder’s cotton rises to 4 on the measurement: 54% of the range, and 227 styles at 100% cotton, against a linen score of 3 at 14%. The authored fabric scores compress at the top and this is the first one corrected against a count.

lede: Eight garments instead of five, and the first brands whose prices have actually been opened and read.
top: Sweater, outerwear and shoes join the five staples. Valstar had all five old slots marked not a staple — a jacket house whose price row said nothing at all. It now reads outerwear $700–4,930. John Smedley's knitwear, its deepest category at 203 products, reads $375–710.

Of the figures that could be compared, 28 of 33 were wrong. A further six carried a price for a garment the house does not make: Incotex makes no t-shirts and no polos, Gran Sasso and Berluti no denim. Where the file was right it was right to the dollar.
Twenty-four brands have been checked properly and eighteen now carry a checked mark beside their prices, meaning all eight garments were opened and read on the brand's own site rather than inherited.

items: BOSS was wrong in all five slots — its t-shirt ceiling out by $170 and its jeans by $250. Ralph Lauren Purple Label's whole recorded jeans band sat below the true floor.
Ferragamo's recorded jeans bracketed its five-pocket trousers, which the rule excludes by name; its only real denim is a single point at $1,150.
Golden Goose's men's denim page opens with nine womenswear items, so an unfiltered read gave a ceiling of $1,850 against a true $530.
Hackett is the first sub-brand trap in the file running both directions: its Heritage line sits below the main line at $170 and above it at $305.

Thirty-six figures are the brand's own list price in euros or won rather than US dollars — Brax, Isaia, J.Lindeberg, JiyongKim, Les Deux. They are real findings but cannot share an axis with a dollar, so they wait for a currency decision rather than being converted.

Four cells are held on their own merits: BOSS's knitwear ceiling is a different garment rather than a better one, Berluti and Incotex's denim rest on judgements worth revisiting, and Ferragamo's shoe ceiling was read from 21 of 226 products.
The price bars were colour-coded across five hues while the rows were already labelled, so the colour read as a legend with no key. One colour now.

In the boutiques index the shop name now wraps and the report action holds its line. Letting the row wrap dropped the button onto its own row for the longer names, so a list of a hundred shops kept changing shape down the page.

lede: Legibility and keyboard fixes, from an external review of the build.
items: True Luxury was the least legible band on the map. Its gradient opened at a light olive and the brand names are cream, which measured 2.31:1 against a 4.5:1 floor — BOSS, Corneliani, Canali and everything else down the left edge. The sweep now opens at the colour that used to sit 18% along, giving 4.56:1 at its lightest and 10.6:1 by the right-hand end.

The search pill was drawn over the brand card. The pill sits at z-index 80 and the card at 60, so a pinned card had it laid across the price chart. It now withdraws for the card as well as for the full-screen views, and the class that hides it is derived from the card's own state rather than set by hand in four places — one of which was stripping it 50 milliseconds after the click.
The brand card was marked up as a tooltip. A 440px panel carrying links and a close button is a dialog, and it now says so.
Escape closes the brand card from anywhere, not only when focus is still in the map grid, and a dismissed card no longer leaves its brand marked as selected.
The focus ring on Clear all was the same green as the button underneath it. It is now cream with a dark halo.

The brand card follows its brand. It is positioned once against the row it belongs to, and was then left there — scroll and it floated over the footer, detached from what it described. It now re-places on scroll and on resize, keeping its eight-pixel gap and switching sides when the room does.
The β badges sat fourteen pixels past the pill they belong to, orphaned in the rail gutter. They now sit inside the label as a superscript.
The masthead was indented four pixels against a rail at zero, which left the whole page reading ragged down its left edge.

lede: Housekeeping in the rail: the channel chips come out, the two-way dials come together, and every group opens on arrival.
items: The channel chips are removed. Own stores was documented as reconciled against the door record and had drifted sixteen brands out of step — eleven claiming own retail against a verified zero, five with doors and no chip. Independents predates the stockist register entirely: 36 brands have named shops with addresses and no chip to show for it. They return when both can be derived from the door and stockist records rather than hand-authored.
All three dial groups now open on arrival rather than Focus alone.
The four two-way dials sit together at the foot of the rail. They read differently from the rest — a centre and two poles rather than a threshold — and were scattered through Focus.
Golfiness is retired as a dial. Its scores remain on the brand cards.
Prices and Boutiques share a row instead of stacking, down to about 380px where they wrap rather than push the page sideways.
The group count badges are derived from the rail instead of being written by hand, so a dial changing group can no longer leave a wrong number behind.
The bands no longer repeat their price range and posture under the name — the prices overlay says it better, and the map is quieter without it.
The $20 tee and $1,000 tee bookends are gone from under the map.
Clear all sits above the dials rather than below them. At the foot of a rail this long it was off-screen whenever it was wanted.

Every boutique in the index carries a report-a-visit action, going to the same prefilled form as the one on its own page — outlined rather than filled, because a hundred solid buttons would be the loudest thing on the page.

Stores, not doors. ‘Door’ is trade usage and reads as jargon to anyone outside it. The word is gone from the interface and from twelve brands’ city lines. It survives where it is ordinary English — the department store next door to McNeil & Reedy on Merchants Row.
The regional control is a filled green pill again rather than a text link. As a link it read as a footnote, and it is the way out of a card to the thing the card is about.

On a phone the brand card is a bottom sheet, and opening the regional panel from it now slides the sheet away rather than stacking two full-screen things on top of each other. The label drops its chevron and the pill is shorter with a mouse than under a thumb.

The search pill belongs to the map and now withdraws behind every overlay. The rule that hides it had been written when there were three full-screen views and never grew with the four added since, so it had been floating over the dial explainer, the regional panel, the stockist pages and the boutiques index.

Overlay headings leave room for the close button. A title long enough to wrap ran underneath it — “Vuori — the Northeast” on a phone — and the fault was invisible to any check comparing element boxes, because a heading always spans its column whatever its text does.

lede: The release where the map stops describing menswear and starts telling you where to buy it.
top: 3,273 doors, addressed. The store record went from 1,898 doors to 3,273, and from 124 brands with a complete record to 185. Four brands were 70% of the old backlog — Levi's, Banana Republic, Polo Ralph Lauren and BOSS — and all four are closed.

Independent stockists, for the first time. A brand with no shop of its own is not a brand you cannot buy. Jack Victor has no US door and trades in eighteen New England towns; its card used to read none — complete. 100 shops, 393 brand-shop pairs, every one linked to a map at its address.
Every dial explains itself. Click a dial's name for what it measures, who holds it, and at what level — with each brand a link through to its own card.
Eleven brands seated, two new dials, and 67 brands now tell you how to say their name.

items: Still a prototype, and still brand-owned US doors plus independent stockists only — no department stores. The stockist register covers the Northeast and nothing else, and every panel says so: a shop outside that footprint is absent because the register has not reached it, not because it does not exist.
the Northeast appears on every brand card, hover card and why card that has a record. It opens a panel listing every door by state, own stores first, each linking to a map at its address.
Boutiques, a new masthead pill, indexes all 100 independent shops by state — town, subtype and how many of the map's brands each carries.

Every stockist has its own page. Where it is, when it was founded, who owns it, and how it started: Darien Sport Shop opened in 1946 by a 22-year-old just back from the South Pacific, on his father's suggestion. 81 of the 100 have their story written, each with its source and a confidence rating. The other 19 say they are researched and not yet written up rather than showing nothing.
Been in lately? Each stockist page carries a visit form, opening with the state and the shop already selected, so anyone standing in a door can report what is on the floor.

The store record is stricter than it was. 29 brands were marked complete and were nothing of the sort — Carhartt read complete at one door against a real 68. Six more were promoted on counts the source itself called unreliable. Both classes are now incomplete, which is a worse-looking number and a truer one.
Banana Republic 294 → 129. The single largest overstatement on the map.
Brooks Brothers 138 → 54. Eighty-eight of those doors were Factory outlets, carried as full-price since before the outlet rule existed.
Paul & Shark now reads zero own doors. The map held its twenty shop-in-shops as its own retail; they never were. That conflict had been open since the first locations pass.
Charles Tyrwhitt closes at 13. It appeared in no tracking file at all and carried an unverified zero — the one genuine hole in the record rather than a disputed number.
Zegna 6 → 26 and Brunello Cucinelli 3 → 34. Both had read as complete. Not every correction goes down.

scandi man. A register, not a passport: Eton is Swedish since 1928 and scores 2 because it sells English shirt formality, while Jil Sander, Lemaire and Margaret Howell score without a Nordic connection at all. NN07 sits one below the top because its name means No Nationality and the map would rather record that tension than flatten it.
bri'ish. Twenty-three brands. Rubinacci scores because Gennaro named his Neapolitan house London House; Vollebak barely does, because its register is materials science and not Britain.

Every dial name is now lower case, and clicking one opens a full explainer — the rubric, everyone who holds it grouped by score, and a standing note that a zero on a register means the register is not represented rather than that nobody looked.
Two-way dials were losing their whole negative half in the explainer, and the not-assessed sentinel was rendering as a score of 99 with 187 brands under it. Both fixed.
Eleven seated: A Bathing Ape, Brax, Easy Mondays, Etro, Golden Goose, Hackett, J.Lindeberg, Les Deux, Rakho, Redvanly and Samsøe Samsøe.

67 brands carry a pronunciation — Hermès (air-MEZ), Jacquemus (zhak-MOOSE), Charles Tyrwhitt (TIRR-it), Wythe (WITH). Shown wherever a brand name appears. A brand without one has not been assessed rather than judged easy.

Hackett's one thing is the logo polo because Jeremy Hackett, asked that exact question in an interview, named it. Golden Goose's is the distressed leather jacket, not the Super-Star — the sneaker sits in the shoe slot, where it belongs.
85 price cells are unassessed, and a full pass across eight garment slots — adding sweater, outerwear and shoes — is briefed and not yet run.
The stockist register stops at the Northeast. Everything beyond it is unknown, not empty.
Brunello Cucinelli is the only brand with a count and no addresses: its source file carries the city in the wrong column, three files running.
Department stores are absent entirely. For 32 brands that is the only physical channel, so their reach reads narrower here than it is.

lede: A chip carousel for the dials, a much smaller header on a phone, and two new two-way dials.
items: Bruv ↔︎ Bruh added, a third two-way dial. It asks which street a brand belongs to rather than which passport it holds: Stone Island is made in Italy and sits at the bruv pole because its home is English terraces, and Polo sits on the bruh side because the Lo Lifes took it and the house had no say. 21 brands called; the rest show a dash and fail the filter at both ends.

The prototype marker is now a single β rather than a boxed BETA, and on a dial it hangs outside the pill in the rail gutter. It had been sitting inside the fixed label column, competing for the same width that keeps all thirty tracks in line — “Bruv ↔︎ Bruh BETA” would have pushed its own track out of alignment. Hovering it still gives the full statement of what has and has not been assessed.
Culture now holds fifteen dials.

The filter rail on a phone was laid out as a wrapping row, so the collapsed groups sat side by side — Fabric and Culture shared a line with Clear All and read as a broken row of fragments. It is a column now.
The rail also drew the browser's own disclosure triangle next to a chevron the design already had, so the group headers rendered as “▼FOCUS10›”. The native marker is suppressed.

The count of matching brands used to stick to the bottom of the rail while it scrolled, covering the last two dials with a green bar. The Filters button carries that count now, so the bar sits at the end of the rail instead of hovering over it.

On a phone the brand card could still open as a floating panel across the masthead rather than as a sheet. A tap on iOS fires a synthetic mouseover, so the hover path runs on touch — and that path positioned the card against the brand, while the sheet layout was attached to the pinned state a tap only reaches on the second press. Any card shown at phone size is now a sheet.

The brand sheet on a phone would not scroll, and covered the whole screen while doing it. A rule written for a floating card taller than the window — cap it to the window height — sat after the two sheet breakpoints at the same weight, so it beat their 62% and 82% caps. The sheet grew to within sixteen pixels of full height, which both buried the page behind it and made its content fit exactly, so there was nothing left to scroll. The window-height rule is now scoped to the case it was written for.

A compact dial strip on phones. The map is about 2,900 pixels tall on a phone, so the rail and the spectrum could never usefully share a screen — opening the filters meant losing sight of the thing being filtered. The strip pins one dial to the bottom of the screen, about 53 pixels tall, and leaves the rest to the map: drag it and the brand names resize in front of you. Arrows step through all thirty-one dials, the label opens the full rail, and it stays in step in both directions, so a change made in the rail comes back to the strip and Clear All resets it. It stands down whenever the rail, a brand card or an overlay is open.

The dials were hard to move with a thumb. They carried the browser's default touch handling, which holds a drag back to decide whether it is a page scroll first — so anything less than a perfectly horizontal drag scrolled the page instead of moving the dial. A drag that starts on a dial now belongs to the dial. In the rail a vertical drag still scrolls the rail, since the rail is mostly sliders and taking the whole gesture would leave nothing to scroll it by. On a touch screen the handles are also larger: 20 pixels in the rail, 24 in the strip, against 13 for a cursor.

Following “full brand details” from a brand card left the card open on top of the page it had just opened, so the same brand appeared twice on one screen. On a desktop the panel covered the card and nobody noticed; on a phone the card is a sheet at the foot of the screen and sat there in plain sight. A full-screen panel now replaces the card rather than sharing the screen with it.

The slider handles sat above their own line in Safari. Chrome puts a slider's track at the top of its box and Safari centres it, and the handle was being positioned by a negative offset tuned against Chrome — correct in one engine, high by several pixels in the other. The track now fills the box with the visible line painted down its middle, so the handle's centre and the line's centre are the same place by construction rather than by adjustment. Measured at zero offset.

Two arrows were drawing as emoji on iOS: the one in the Bruv ↔ Bruh label and the one marking an outbound link, both appearing as blue tiles rather than as type. Unicode gives those characters an emoji presentation by default and a text presentation only on request, so both now ask for it explicitly.

Charles Tyrwhitt seated in Premium, the 187th brand. Mail order from a Bristol student room in 1986, a Jermyn Street shop by 1997 and Madison Avenue by 2002; the non-iron shirt is the whole proposition and the multibuy is how it is actually sold. Its one thing is the non-iron twill shirt, $129 listed and $74.75 in a multibuy. Only the dress shirt carries a price — the other four staples show a question mark, because one figure from one product page is a figure, not a range.

Lacoste enumerated: 28 full-price US doors across 25 towns, and 15 outlets recorded separately. The brand's own locator labels every door as a boutique, a flagship or an outlet, so the two are separated at source rather than guessed from the town — which matters, because five towns turn out to be the opposite of what their names suggest. San Diego and West Palm Beach are outlet only. Chicago and Miami hold both. The count of 91 that stood here before was the all-format number, outlets included, and has been replaced.
Lacoste has no full-price door in the Boston market, which the locator states plainly: Massachusetts returns Wrentham and nothing else.

Two more places where quiet was made with opacity rather than colour, both on the brand page: the line reading “not a staple” measured 1.95:1, and the one reading “not assessed” was little better. Neither had shown up before because the pages being checked happened not to contain either. All 187 brand pages have now been swept rather than sampled.

TravisMathew enumerated and complete: 57 full-price US doors across 54 towns, every one with a street address from the brand's own locator. The locator lists 67 in all — six US outlets and four international doors were separated out and are recorded rather than dropped. The line here previously read “40+ stores”.

Two conventions arrived with that work and are worth keeping. A door can now be marked excluded with a reason rather than being deleted, so an outlet or a Tokyo shop stays visible as a decision. And a fleet count can state its scope precisely — US, full-price, own-store — rather than only US or global, which is the distinction the Lacoste count of 91 fell down on.

The search pill tucks to the right on a phone. It had been a 130-pixel bar floating over the map at all times, in front of whichever brands happened to be under it; it is now a 44-pixel disc at the edge that opens to the full-width field on a tap and closes again once a brand is found. The expanded state already existed for typing — this only changes what it looks like when it is not being used.

The price-and-posture line beside each band name is hidden on narrow screens. It wrapped to two and three lines and pushed the band name off its own row, and the band name is what a reader needs there — the explanation belongs to the wider layout and to the prices overlay. Measured at every width from 701 upward: Accessible Luxury is the last to stop wrapping, at 940 pixels, so that is where the line returns.

The brand sheet can be swiped away. It follows the finger, springs back if the pull is short, and closes past about a quarter of its height — and it only takes over the gesture when the sheet is already at its top, so flicking through the card's own content still scrolls it. A grab handle sits above the text to say so. The close button and a tap outside both still work.
Version numbers move to three parts — major, minor, patch. Earlier entries have been relabelled to match; the releases themselves are unchanged.

The search field opened in the wrong place. The offset that keeps the collapsed disc clear of the dial strip was written after the rule that lifts the field above the keyboard, and beat it — so the field never followed the keyboard at all and sat stranded in the middle of the screen with the dial strip still showing beneath it. The offset now applies only while the search is closed, and the strip stands down while it is open.
Escape cleared the search field but never let go of it, so the search stayed open with the keyboard gone. A second Escape now closes it.

Dries Van Noten's one thing changed from a printed shirt to the jacquard wool hat — $325, five colourways, earflaps and braided ties. The shirt entry pointed at a site search rather than a garment; the hat is a specific object on the house's own page, and it is the pattern habit at its smallest scale, the one piece where the colour is the whole argument rather than a garment carrying it. Seen in the Paris window.
Its city line read “LA store” while the door record held two, Los Angeles and New York. The prose was behind the data.

Opening the search on an iPhone zoomed the whole page. Safari enlarges the page whenever a focused field is set below sixteen pixels, and this one was thirteen — so the layout scaled up around it and everything ran off the right edge. The field is sixteen pixels now, which is the threshold, and nothing zooms.
The search field drew two rings when focused, its own border and a focus outline outside it. The focus mark is now a soft halo on the same control rather than a second box around it.

Dragging a dial made the page flash. The why cards are a large block that sits above the map and pushes it down, and they were being torn down and rebuilt on every step of a drag — appearing at two matches, vanishing at eleven, reappearing at eight, several times a second. The map still filters live; the panel now waits for the drag to settle. Thirteen steps of a drag produce one rebuild rather than thirteen.

Baracuta's one thing now points at the house's own G9 Harrington collection rather than a site search. The note on it had said best-guess, verify — for a brand whose whole identity is one named jacket, that was the wrong place to leave a guess.

Sail ↔︎ Power added, a fourth two-way dial. It asks which kind of boating rather than how much of it, which is what Boat already measures. The case for it was sitting in the notes: Kiton and Hermès both score five on Boat and belong at opposite ends here — one is the deck of something you are driven to, the other is a house that began with harness and took up sailing. Ten brands called, from Sease and Paul & Shark at the sail end to Zilli and Stefano Ricci at the crewed-deck end.

The sheet showed a grab handle but would not actually be pulled down. The gesture was registered as a passive listener, which cannot stop the browser doing its own thing — so iOS ran its elastic bounce on the card's contents while the code tried to move the card, and neither won. The pull now takes the gesture properly once it starts from the top of the sheet, and the handle is larger.

The dial strip moves to the top and becomes a carousel. Rather than one dial behind a pair of arrows, all thirty-two sit in a scrolling row of chips: each carries its dial's colour, any that is filtering is filled in and shows its setting, and tapping one brings up its slider underneath. The set is visible at a glance and none of it is more than a tap away.

The header on a phone was 183 pixels tall — with the button and the rule beneath it, 244 pixels, or 29% of the screen, gone before the map began. The title and the prices button now share a row and the title stops being a poster. The header is 47 pixels and the whole of the chrome is 187, carousel included.

A Clear button in the filter row, next to All. It appears only when something is actually filtering — a dial, a channel chip or a search — so it never sits there as a dead control taking width from the slider, and it clears all three at once.

The two-way dials flickered while being dragged. A filter pass rescans all 187 brands and rewrites their type sizes, about ten milliseconds, and a mouse drag asks for one roughly sixty times a second — so a pass never finished before the next arrived. The map now redraws once a frame however fast the dial moves, while the reading beside it stays live. Thirteen steps of a drag produce one redraw rather than thirteen. It showed on the two-way dials first because zero sits in the middle of their travel, so every drag across the range passed through the unfiltered map on the way; at one redraw a frame a quick drag no longer draws it at all.

The why cards moved below the map. They had been sitting above it and they are tall — 1,372 pixels for seven brands — so every time they appeared or went away the whole spectrum was thrown 1,400 pixels down the page and hauled back. On a two-way dial, where the count crosses the ten-brand threshold repeatedly on the way across, that happened several times a second and read as the map flickering. Below the map they can come and go without moving it: measured across a full drag, the spectrum now holds one position where it previously alternated between two. They are also no longer blanked while a drag is in progress — holding the previous answer for a moment is better than blinking.

The map thrashed while a dial was being dragged. Brand names carry their weight from the filter as well as their size, and both were being animated over 280 milliseconds — and both change how wide a word is. So every adjustment set 187 names reflowing continuously for the length of the animation, and in a layout that wraps, moving one name moves all of them. Measured on a real drag: 186 of 187 names changed position on every step. Only the fading is animated now, and while a dial is actually being held the map dims and undims but holds its layout, with the sizes arriving when the dial is let go. The same drag now moves nothing at all until release.

The map holds still while a dial is moving, whatever is moving it. Type size carries the score, so resizing reflows the whole wrapped map — one step moved 186 of 187 names. The map already held its layout during a mouse drag, but the hold was keyed to the pointer, so every other way of working a dial went straight through it: arrow keys on a focused slider repositioned around 180 names on every press. The hold is now driven by the changes themselves and released once they stop, or when the button comes up. Measured across a drag: nothing moves until it ends.

The dial moved out from under the cursor while it was being used. Filtering changes the map's height — fewer, smaller names wrap into fewer rows — and the why cards add up to 1,372 pixels below it, so the page grew and shrank with every adjustment. The browser then shifted the scroll position to compensate, and the filter rail, which sticks within the same container, travelled with it: measured while scrolled, the dial moved 171 pixels the moment a drag ended. Three things now hold it still. The page no longer re-anchors while the map is being filtered. The map reserves its full height, so filtering cannot shrink it. And the cards sit outside the layout the rail lives in, capped so they scroll within themselves rather than lengthening the page. Measured through a drag while scrolled: the dial does not move at all, before or after release.

The sliders changed width as they were used. The track flexed and the reading beside it did not, so a dial saying “specialist care” had a 66-pixel track and the same dial saying “off” had 112 — the handle shifted under the finger as the word grew. The track is a fixed width now and the reading takes what is left; all thirty-two are identical and start at the same point. Four of the longest readings were shortened to fit rather than being cut off.

Two dials pulled to opposite ends could empty the map. The guard that stops a setting leaving nothing on screen counted only settings above zero and always compared upwards, so a two-way dial at its negative end was invisible to it and unprotected. It now uses the same rule the map uses and steps back from whichever end the dial is at. Every pair of two-way dials in both directions, every two-way dial against every other dial at full, and all four two-way dials at once: no combination empties the map.

A channel could still empty the map. The guard that stops a setting leaving nothing on screen only ever knew about the dials; channel is a second filter applied on top of them, so choosing one could clear a map the dials had been carefully kept populated — fourteen combinations did. Choosing a channel now checks the whole filter, and if nothing would survive the dials give way one step at a time, starting with whichever is set hardest. The channel is the choice just made, so it is the one that stands.

Maison Margiela repriced across all five staples, against the house's own US pages. The floors had been coming from MM6, the cheaper line that shares the same website: the recorded t-shirt started at $385 when nothing on the mainline sells below $520, and the dress shirt started at $590 when nothing sells below $785. The ceilings were low too — shirts run to $1,430 rather than the $1,175 recorded. Jeans and trousers had a single figure each rather than a range, and the trouser figure of $1,885 was above anything now on sale. Two tailored shirts at $2,375 and $2,245 and a double-layer at $1,790 are excluded as different constructions rather than dearer versions of the same shirt.

First return from the price audit: 24 cells corrected against live retail, across BOSS, Thom Browne, Giorgio Armani, Saint Laurent, Givenchy, McQueen, Junya Watanabe, Fear of God, Isaia, Incotex, Drake's, Suitsupply, RRL, Robert Barakett, Margaret Howell and Charles Tyrwhitt. Thirteen of the twenty-four single figures standing in for ranges are now ranges.

BOSS was the worst of it, as expected: all five staples wrong, because the recorded figures had HUGO mixed in — a cheaper brand on the same website. Trousers ran $140–230 and actually run $199–599. It is the same fault Maison Margiela had with MM6 and Ralph Lauren Purple Label has with the wider Ralph Lauren catalogue: a floor picked up from a cheaper line sharing a shop.
Isaia's t-shirt had been recorded at $595, which is not the price of any Isaia t-shirt — it is the price of an Isaia sweater. Cross-category rather than cross-line, but the same kind of mistake.

Taylor Stitch completed from the house's own about page: three stores with street addresses, two of them in San Francisco where the record had one. Its one thing, the Jack shirt, now points at the collection rather than a site search — and the page makes the case for it, since the house calls itself a shirting company at its core and cites 22 stitches per inch and French seams as what it learnt from the oldest family of shirtmakers in the country.

lede: The first release where every brand states how well it is known.

items: Treat this as a prototype. It covers brand-owned US doors only — no wholesale, no department-store carriage, no neighbourhoods — and 59 of 186 brands are still short of a complete door list. What it will not do is guess: nothing here is inferred from a plausible number.
US own-store footprint added, verified brand by brand against store locators, brand statements and structured page data. 1,840 doors across 186 brands.

Every brand reads as complete, incomplete or not checked. 127 brands are complete, meaning every door is enumerated with a street address and a citable source; 44 are partial; 15 carry a sourced fleet count with the addresses still to come.
Zero US doors is a result, not a blank. Ted Baker, Criquet, Aspesi, Charvet, Cuts Clothing, Margaret Howell, Percival and others read as none, checked.
Ted Baker's line said major metros and department stores. Its entire North American operation was liquidated in May 2024, 34 doors. The map was pointing at shops that closed two years ago.
Criquet's line named an Austin store on South First Street. The brand's own help centre calls it their only door, and it is closed.
Jil Sander was recorded as having no US stores. It has two, on Madison Avenue and in Beverly Hills, both opened after the original research.
Percival confirmed at three London shops and no US doors.
The city line and the store record no longer say the same thing twice. The city line carries the channel — who else sells the brand — and the store record carries the doors.

122 brands read as complete, 49 partial, 15 as a count with the addresses still to come. Five records that reconciled on their own numbers were demoted anyway, because the city line above them named metros the door list did not contain — Kiton, Kith's neighbour Thom Browne, Casablanca, Missoni and James Perse, whose line claims about forty stores against three found.

Two channel filters were labelled with meanings the data does not carry. “Online only” held 37 brands, 21 of which also run their own stores — Everlane with eight doors, Sid Mashburn with eight, and Polo Ralph Lauren. It means sells direct, and now reads Direct. “Off-price” held Levi's and J.Crew at one end and Junya Watanabe, Wales Bonner and Fedeli at the other; what every member shares is being sold through third-party online retailers, so it now reads E-tail.

The own-stores filter was reconciled against the verified door record, which disagreed with it on 22 brands. Eight with confirmed US doors were missing from it — Eton, Herno, Boglioli, Cesare Attolini, NN07, Purple, Joe's Jeans, Rhoback. Eleven with a checked zero were wrongly in it. Three more looked wrong and were not: a verified zero storefronts is not the same as no own presence, and Fear of God's LA flagship, Incotex at Slowear in New York and Rubinacci's by-appointment room in New York all stay.
Open conflict, left visible rather than settled: Fear of God's city line names an LA flagship and the locations pass records zero US doors. Both cannot be right.

Complete. All 180 brands that existed when the pass ran were verified at least once against brand sites and full-price retail listings. The six seated afterwards, plus two Fear of God garments with no reliable listing, carry a question mark rather than an estimate.

Staple prices reverified end to end across five passes. 424 of 900 figures moved: Tom Ford's tee ceiling from $650 to $3,990, Hermès' dress shirt from $1,400 to $4,750, Yohji Yamamoto's dress pants down from $1,100 to $364.
Sixty-five cells that read as not a staple were wrong — the brand does make the garment. Ten carried a price for something not in the line.
A third price state. A figure is a checked range, an em dash is a checked absence, and a question mark means nobody has looked yet.

The outliers rule is written down rather than decided brand by brand: the same silhouette in a premium fabric counts as the ceiling, a different construction or a named capsule does not. Hermès' $4,750 silk shirt is in; its $17,100 exotic-skin trouser is out.
Staple prices promoted to the masthead. It had been reachable only from the axis label and a footer link, neither of which reads as a way in.

All 186 brands now carry an entry. The last twelve were red-pen calls: Rowan's Asher tee, Barbour's Bedale over its Beaufort, Filson's Mackinaw Cruiser, the Ralston jean, Sandro's leather biker, the Martini fit, Rockstud Untitled, Jil Sander's poplin shirt, the Husbands peak-lapel jacket and Patrick James' house-label sport coat.

Two are deliberate absences. Jacquemus and Givenchy were checked and found to have no signature garment — Jacquemus attaches to collections and bags rather than a recurring model, and Givenchy's Shark Lock, which reads as the obvious answer, is womenswear.

Corneliani corrected to the Identity Jacket, pointing at the house's own page for the model rather than an Italian-language search result. John Smedley sharpened from the Sea Island polo to the Adrian, which is what the house calls it.
Shoes is a prototype: 74 of 186 brands assessed. The rest show a dash, which means nobody has looked, not that the brand makes no shoes.
Golffice added, a two-way dial running from the boardroom end to the back nine. 79 brands scored.

Shoes rebuilt on three states: a score, a verified zero, or nothing. The 1 and 2 bands were removed because no brand in them had been checked — a plausible number had been standing in for a looked-at one across 55 brands.
Criquet seated in Premium.

The map is usable without a mouse. All 186 brands were unreachable by keyboard — every one of the page's 77 tab stops was a dial, a chip or a button, and the dataset itself could not be got at, which also put it out of reach of a screen reader. Each band is now a listbox with a single tab stop: arrows move between brands and across bands, up and down move by visual row, Home and End jump to the ends, Enter or Space opens the card and Escape closes it and gives focus back.
A skip link, because the dials came first and reaching the map took 32 tab presses. It is now two.
Brands carry a visible focus ring, and the open one is marked as selected for screen readers. The single tab stop per band is never allowed to land on a brand the filter has excluded.

Hit areas raised. The dial sliders were 132 by 14 pixels; the channel chips and Clear All sat at 28 to 30; the two footer links were 18 tall. Nothing interactive is now under 24 pixels except two brand names that are simply short words.
A type floor. Six label classes ran between 8.5 and 10.5 pixels — dial values, chip counts, group counts, the channel label. All are now 10.5 or above, the beta badge alone excepted at 9.5.

Contrast brought up to standard. Twenty-six pieces of text failed the 4.5:1 minimum, the worst at 2.16:1. The cause was not the colours so much as the method: quietness was being made with opacity, and opacity fades contrast with everything else — a label set at half opacity blended back to 2:1 however dark its colour was. Quietness is now made with colour, which can be measured.
Every focusable element shows a visible focus ring. Forty-six had neither an outline nor a shadow when focused, including the sliders, the group headers and the search box.
Checked at 320 pixels wide and at 200% text: no horizontal scrolling, all 186 brands still rendered. Reduced motion is honoured, and there is no keyboard trap.

The why cards — the panel that appears when a filter narrows the map to ten brands or fewer — were answering a different question from the map beneath them. They kept their own copy of the filter rule, and the copy had drifted three ways: the channel chips were ignored entirely, so filtering to E-tail and Durability 5 dimmed the map to one brand and still drew seven cards; a two-way dial's negative setting was read as a minimum, so asking for the easy end of Ease of Care drew nothing; and a brand nobody had assessed satisfied any threshold, which is the fault the map filter carried until this release. The panel now reads the map's own result rather than deriving its own.

The hover card could cover the row it belonged to. It was placed below the brand, flipped above if that did not fit, and otherwise pinned to the top of the window at whatever height it happened to be — which on a tall window meant a card long enough to bury its own row and several others. The card now goes wholly below the row or wholly above it, and is capped to the space on that side rather than clamped into the window. The row you are reading the card against stays visible.

The three full-screen panels were not modal to a keyboard. Focus never moved into them when they opened, and Tab walked straight past them into the dials behind — fifteen stops out of fifteen landed on controls the reader could not see. Focus now moves in on open, stays inside, and returns to whatever opened it.
The brand page kept the scroll position of the brand before it. Read one to the bottom, follow a link to the next, and the next one opened halfway down.

The left rail had grown a sideways scrollbar. The dial tooltips are 270 pixels wide and were positioned against the 86-pixel label, which is the box they are measured from — so 296 pixels of tooltip sat inside a 278-pixel row, and the rail, which scrolls, counted it. The tooltips are now measured from the row and sized to it, so they fit whatever the rail is wide.

Tapping a brand on a phone did nothing. The card was built and pinned correctly, then hidden 220 milliseconds later: a tap fires a synthetic mouseover followed by a mouseout, and the hover-out handler took the card away without unpinning it. A card opened deliberately is now dismissed only by its close button or a click outside it. The mobile card itself — a bottom sheet with a close button — had been built and styled and was never reachable.

A phone held sideways got no card at all. The bottom sheet was keyed to screen width, and a landscape phone is 844 pixels wide — so it fell through to the desktop treatment, which was never positioned for a pinned card and put it 1,982 pixels down a 390-pixel window. The sheet now answers to height as well as width, and a card taller than the window scrolls.

With the dial rail closed, nothing said a filter was on. The whole rail is hidden when collapsed, so the count of matching brands went with it — and a filtered-out brand does not respond to a tap, which left most of the map silently inert. The Filters button now carries the count and highlights while a filter is running.
A card pinned on a tablet had no way out. The close button was styled only inside the phone breakpoints; tapping outside worked but nothing said so. It now appears on any pinned card at any width.

The Shoes filter was returning every brand nobody had checked. Unassessed dials carry a sentinel value internally, and the filter only excluded it on the two-way dials — Shoes is the first one-way dial to use one, so asking for shoes at 3 or above returned 160 brands when the honest answer is 48. The sentinel now fails every filter, which is what not assessed has to mean.

That same sentinel fed the type-size calculation, which sets a brand's size from its average score across the active dials. A brand name could render at 276px and fill the screen. The calculation is now bounded by the actual scale.

The price scale ran to $2,000 while the reverified data runs to $4,750, so 33 bars extended past the right edge of their track â Hermès' dress shirt computed to 119% of the width. The scale now ends at $5,000, with a gridline added at $3,200.

In the five-garment view, a bar for one of the two cheapest staples on the chart started at the far left of the track and printed on top of its own row label. The labels now sit in a gutter beside the track rather than inside it.
Every dial track was a different length. The row gave the label its natural width and handed the remainder to the slider, so Fit Flexibility ran 135px against Ski's 192px. All thirty now match.
Four dials drew a near-black groove while sitting at zero, because Chrome recolours a native slider track against its accent colour by a rule of its own. The tracks are now drawn explicitly.
The Focus group counted 8 dials against the 10 it holds.
The masthead's mobile rules were sitting inside the reduced-motion query rather than a width breakpoint, so they fired only for reduced-motion users and never on a phone.
Search on a phone matched against the wrong element and returned nothing.
Accented brand names were stored two ways in the same file, so an edit made against one spelling silently skipped the other.
Single-point price reads displayed as a range of a number to itself.
